item.title: Tech supply chains are relocating fragility — not removing it
item.description:
For decades, the technology industry was built around supply chains that were global, but highly concentrated and fragile.

The shifting geopolitical landscape in recent years necessitated an evolution of these supply chains that, on the surface, seem more diversified — but are no less fragile.

Instead of strengthening them, certain aspects of tech supply chains were relocated in ways that created a far higher cost per unit of output.

The result? Supply chains that only relocate fragility while remaining highly concentrated.

This phenomenon poses a threat to the entire tech industry as companies are now paying to run more complex and redundant supply chains while remaining exposed to the same chokepoints as before.

Global reach is not the same as diversification

Let’s clarify something: while the tech industry’s supply chains are often described as global, calling them concentrated occurs less frequently.

Various countries were involved, but each had their own specific task. Advanced logic predominantly came from Taiwan, assembly and most non-chip components came from mainland China — and the equipment to make them came from a short list of vendors in the US, Japan and the Netherlands.

Each of these stages represented concentrated points of potential failure along a highly dependent supply chain.

That structure rested on a political premise as much as an economic one. Concentration created deeper interdependence — which was assumed to be stabilizing since countries that supplied each other’s critical inputs seemingly had too much to lose from interrupting the flow.

However, that understanding has been tested in recent years. Interdependence is increasingly perceived as leverage rather than insurance, and export controls made the shift explicit.

Now, a chokepoint is an instrument that a government may choose to use — and tech supply chains began evolving as more actors used this leverage.

Recent trade data clearly shows this evolution.

The most notable shift happened after the US-China trade war in 2018. China’s share of US electronics imports fell from 52% in 2018 to 37% in 2022 — a 29% decrease in just four years.

In servers, China’s share of global supply fell from over 90% before 2018 to below 50% by 2022. Conversely, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) saw its share rise from 17% in 2018 to 26% in 2022.

In 2025, Vietnam and India surpassed China in share of US smartphone imports, and Vietnam surpassed China in share of US laptop imports.

Marko Markov

This shift in trade and the evolution of tech supply chains manifested itself in two main ways:

  • Companies moved final assembly production to new countries to minimize risk.
  • Governments incentivized production domestically as a way to maximize security and boost economic growth.

While both of these developments were a response to the changing landscape, neither fully addressed the true fragility that decades of concentration have developed.

What is actually moving?

The simplest part of a tech hardware supply chain to move is final assembly. Its primary input is labor and there is not much fixed equipment that needs to be moved.

Countries benefiting from this shift include Vietnam, India, Thailand and Mexico — who all became final assembly hubs and imported greater shares of components from China.

What has not moved is most of what makes the product possible.

Chip fabrication depends on machines only a handful of companies globally know how to build — and on engineers who are scarce everywhere.

Advanced packaging is still overwhelmingly done in East Asia, while specialized components carry their own factories, approvals and suppliers behind them.

None of this can be easily relocated.

What results is an industry that has spent heavily on relocating the layer that was never really the vulnerability, while the concentration of key components remains.

Marko Markov

Governments strike back

Governments around the world reached this same conclusion.

The high-value component layer stayed in place because relocation costs were too high.

A leading-edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars and years to build — a risky investment in a world of increasing disruptions. Very few companies acting commercially would move that layer.

However, the rise of geopolitical uncertainty in recent years — the 2018 US-China trade war, the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the ongoing war in the Middle East — have made governments more inclined to create incentives to move high-value components domestically.

This is where the CHIPS and Science Act factors in as an incentive designed to make an uneconomic location economic.

Whether this is working or not depends on what you are measuring. In May 2024, the Semiconductor Industry Association projected that US fab capacity will grow by 203% by 2032 and that the US will make up 28% of global chip capital expenditures between 2024-2032 — estimated to be approximately $650 billion.

This looks like a success on the surface, but that same report suggests this expenditure and growth will only result in the US share of world chip manufacturing increasing from 10% to 14% by 2032.

Essentially, a quarter of the world’s chip investment results in an increase of four percentage points of output. This suggests that relocating high-value components is far more challenging — even with large sums of government investment.

China, meanwhile, is funding a domestic industry built to run without Western technology. Its third chip fund, launched in 2024, targets high-value components with support totaling $47.5 billion.

Both countries are strongly incentivizing a future industry where high-value components are concentrated domestically in an attempt to create a more secure supply chain.

More complexity at the end of the day

These efforts by companies and governments only added complexity to supply chains instead of removing it.

Companies moved assembly, but not high-value components. Governments are attempting to move high-value components, but with mixed results and within their own borders.

What’s changed?

A wafer made now (or in the future) could be made in Arizona, travel to Asia to be packaged and then return stateside again to be assembled. This ultimately creates more steps, more borders and more paperwork in an already complex supply chain.

That is redundancy that increases costs for technology companies.

TSMC put a number on this when it told investors that running fabs outside Taiwan will reduce gross margin by two-to-three percentage points, widening to three-to-four percentage points as those plants scale.

Most firms would have no cushion. A majority of contract manufacturers work on thin gross margins; when their costs rise, the money most likely needs to come from the customer’s price.

As technology buyers, companies need to start preparing for a world of higher prices — but none of this means the reorientation was a mistake.

A supply chain running through a single strait, a handful of foundries and a short list of tool vendors was a real risk. No business or political leader who lived through 2020 and 2021 was going to sit on their hands, especially as the boom in the promise of AI has provided more pressure on supply chains.

So, what has all this change provided? So far, it’s been an evolution of movement more so than resiliency.

Final assembly relocated because final assembly was always the least expensive thing to move. The layers of concentration that actually constrain the industry — fabrication, advanced packaging and the specialized components that carry their own supplier networks behind them — have barely shifted.

When governments do move them, it’s predominantly through large incentives that have mixed results. The US and China, the world’s two economic superpowers, are now funding separate systems built to avoid depending on each other — and neither is less concentrated and less fragile than before.

Meanwhile, companies suffer from increased supply chain complexity that’s accompanied by increased prices.

The deeper issues remain ingrained in the system — and those in the tech industry should stop mistaking a redrawn map for a rebuilt supply chain.

item.title: A decision hiding in plain sight
item.description:
Picture two retail chains. Akkar & Co Group is the giant — hundreds of stores, the biggest revenue in the sector, the name every shopper recognizes. Tripoli Boutique is the smaller player — a regional chain with a loyal but modest footprint, competing against Akkar & Co’s sheer size. Both start the same way: manual inventory counts, paper-based reordering, spreadsheets stitched together by exhausted store managers — no real digital backbone anywhere.

Then both decide it’s time to grow up, picking the same cloud ERP platform and hiring the same systems integrator (SI) to implement it. Same software, same partner, same rough timeline — on paper, Akkar & Co and Tripoli Boutique are starting the race from the exact same line.

But one choice splits their paths. Akkar & Co asks for the system to be heavily customized around its own way of doing things — its own merchandising logic, its own supplier terms, its own store-level workflows. It has a simple conviction behind the request: our processes are the reason we’re winning, and no off-the-shelf system should be allowed to flatten them. Tripoli Boutique, without that same conviction — or the budget to test it — accepts the standard, out-of-the-box configuration the SI recommends.

Three years later, where do these two retailers actually stand — and what does that tell us about the risk of believing your own processes are worth defending?

The fork in the road

Because the software and the implementer are identical, we can rule those out as reasons for whatever happens next. The one real variable is a decision: bend the software to fit the business, or bend the business to fit the software.

Akkar & Co takes the first path, with confidence rather than stubbornness. Leadership had spent years refining exactly how the company merchandises, prices, and replenishes stores — habits and judgment calls that made it the biggest name in the category. “The ERP should adapt to us, not the other way round,” the CIO tells the board, “Because what we do isn’t generic, and we’re not going to let a piece of software pretend otherwise.” So Akkar & Co asks for custom pricing engines, custom store-replenishment logic, custom loyalty integrations — everything tailored to encode what actually makes it good at retail.

Tripoli Boutique takes the second path, and it’s worth being honest about why. It isn’t just budget. Tripoli Boutique has never been entirely sure its own processes are anything special — it has grown steadily, but never by doing anything a competitor couldn’t copy. Standard configuration isn’t a disciplined strategic choice so much as the safer, cheaper default for a company that has never had the confidence, or the resources, to bet that its own way of working is worth preserving in code.

That difference — conviction versus caution — is the whole story.

Two go-lives, one clear fit

Akkar & Co’s go-live is hard. Customization means a longer project, a bigger bill, and more testing when real store data — SKUs, promotions, seasonal pricing — hits a system built to order. Change management is heavy too, because store staff are being asked to fully commit to a tool built around exactly how they already work. But once it stabilizes, the system fits Akkar & Co like a tailored suit, because it was cut from Akkar & Co’s own pattern. Store managers don’t just tolerate it — they recognize their own judgment reflected back at them in how the system behaves.

This isn’t a small footnote. A 2025 report on ERP customization costs found most ERP implementations cost three to four times the original budget, and that modifications made “to improve usability” — the polite name for customization — drive the overspend in roughly two out of three projects. Akkar & Co walks into that statistic with open eyes. For a company confident in what it’s protecting, the extra spend isn’t a risk. It’s the price of keeping an edge intact.

Tripoli Boutique’s go-live, by contrast, is smooth and cheap — and unremarkable. Standard configuration means fewer surprises and a shorter timeline. Staff adjust to the system’s way of doing things because there was never really a “Tripoli Boutique way” strong enough to insist on keeping. It works fine. It just doesn’t do anything for the company that a hundred other retailers on the same platform aren’t already doing.

The AI divide

About a year or two after go-live, the ERP vendor rolls out its next big wave of features — built-in AI: demand forecasting, anomaly detection, automated markdown suggestions, a copilot for store performance questions. This is not a separate project either retailer asked for. It’s simply the next version of the software both of them already own. But what each company gets out of it depends entirely on what it built underneath.

For Tripoli Boutique, the AI is a wash. Because its configuration is standard, the AI slots in cleanly and works well — genuinely useful for demand forecasting and reordering. But it’s the same AI every other retailer running the same standard setup gets. It doesn’t help Tripoli Boutique stand out. It helps Tripoli Boutique keep up, and nothing more.

For Akkar & Co, the AI becomes something else entirely. Because the vendor’s AI learns from the data and workflows underneath it, and Akkar & Co’s data and workflows encode three years of genuinely differentiated retail judgment — pricing logic built around real customer behavior, replenishment rules shaped by real store-level patterns — Akkar & Co’s AI comes out sharper. It doesn’t just forecast demand; it starts predicting the shape of a customer’s experience: what a shopper is likely to want next, when they’re likely to want it, what would make them spend more or come back sooner. The same AI feature, running on top of a genuinely superior foundation, produces a genuinely superior result. This is the payoff the customization was always betting on.

A 2026 industry briefing on ERP and generative AI makes a related point: the retailers getting the most out of AI aren’t necessarily the ones with the newest technology, but the ones whose underlying data and processes were distinctive enough to give the AI something worth learning from in the first place. Generic input, generic output. Distinctive input, distinctive output. Akkar & Co bet on distinctive input three years earlier, without knowing exactly what it would pay off as.

3 years later: the scoreboard

So, three years on — who’s ahead?

Akkar & Co is not just still leading; the lead has grown. That lines up with the broader market too: the biggest ERP vendors and their biggest customers tend to stay on top for a long stretch, and current global ERP market data shows the same concentration pattern, with the largest players controlling a disproportionate share of a market still growing at double digits every year. Size, once earned, tends to keep earning — but this time, faster.

A few things are true at once:

  • Momentum was never really at risk. Market leadership built over years — brand trust, customer relationships, scale, supplier power — was always going to be hard for Tripoli Boutique to close in three years. But the ERP decision didn’t just fail to shrink that gap. It widened it.
  • The customization was the whole point, not a side bet. Akkar & Co’s custom workflows encoded genuine competitive advantage — pricing logic, replenishment rules, merchandising judgment that actually differentiate the business. When AI arrived, that advantage didn’t just survive the upgrade. It compounded through it.
  • Tripoli Boutique’s caution had a ceiling. Lower cost and a smoother go-live were real, honest advantages in year one. But without a genuine edge underneath its systems, Tripoli Boutique had nothing for the AI wave to amplify. Standard configuration kept it safe. It never once made it distinctive.
  • The gap that might have narrowed didn’t. In a story where Tripoli Boutique’s agility slowly closes the distance, this isn’t that story. Akkar & Co’s AI-driven differentiation opened a second front Tripoli Boutique had no way to compete on, on top of the first one it was already losing.

Akkar & Co is ahead because of the customization, not in spite of the cost and friction it created going in. The bet on “our processes are superior” turned out to be correct, and correct bets compound.

Image is everything

Once Akkar & Co’s AI started genuinely shaping the customer experience — not just the back office — the company didn’t stay quiet about it. It built a one-year, aggressive marketing campaign around it. Customer-facing stories about AI that seemed to know what a shopper wanted before they did. Public demonstrations of personalized recommendations, faster and more relevant than anything a shopper had seen from a competitor. Messaging that made a simple, confident claim: this is what happens when a retailer’s technology is built around genuinely better judgment.

This wasn’t a defensive move. Akkar & Co wasn’t reacting to a closing gap — there wasn’t one to close. It was amplifying a real advantage it already had. And it worked, for a very ordinary reason: shoppers don’t audit a retailer’s back-end systems, but they do notice when a store seems to understand them better than the last one did, and they talk about it. A 2026 review of branding statistics found that the large majority of marketing executives consider branding essential to business growth, and that companies with consistent, visible branding see measurably higher revenue growth than those without it — branding ROI shows up directly in customer lifetime value and market share, not just recognition. None of this proves marketing alone drove Akkar & Co’s growth — but paired with a genuine capability underneath it, the campaign didn’t need to invent a story. It only had to tell a true one, loudly.

Technology gave Akkar & Co something real to say. Marketing made sure everyone heard it.

The long game

Here’s the part nobody outside Akkar & Co’s boardroom saw coming. Buried in Akkar & Co’s five-year strategic plan, quietly sitting behind the public narrative of “AI leadership,” was a single line item: acquire Tripoli Boutique.

It wasn’t about market share — Tripoli Boutique’s share was modest enough that absorbing it barely moved Akkar & Co’s numbers. What Akkar & Co wanted was something its own mass-market base could never give it: Tripoli Boutique’s customers. Despite its unremarkable technology, Tripoli Boutique had spent 20 years quietly building a small but genuinely valuable clientele — customers with serious money, who bought high-end jewelry and premium cosmetics, and who trusted Tripoli Boutique’s staff enough to keep coming back for exactly that kind of purchase. It was a relationship built the old way, person to person, long before either company touched an ERP system.

Akkar & Co’s leadership recognized that value the moment its own AI proved what it could do with distinctive data. Feed 20 years of high-value jewelry and cosmetics purchase history into an AI engine already sharp enough to predict ordinary shoppers’ behavior, and something bigger becomes possible: a premium tier Akkar & Co could never have built organically, and a much clearer picture of exactly which VIP customers were worth a personal call, a private preview, or a nudge toward the next expensive purchase.

Tripoli Boutique’s board wasn’t blind to the timing. They’d turned down Akkar & Co’s interest twice before, confident their customer relationships were worth more standing alone. This time, watching a competitor’s AI-driven personalization pull further ahead every quarter with no real answer of their own, the board concluded that their most valuable asset — the trust of their VIP customers — would do more good inside a company that could finally act on it at scale than it would sitting inside a smaller one that couldn’t. It wasn’t a surrender. It was a recognition that the asset and the capability to use it well finally belonged in the same building.

The deal wouldn’t be frictionless in real life — a regulator would want a look at combined market share in overlapping regions, and any acquisition of this size rarely closes without scrutiny — but in this telling, the story is about strategy, not scrutiny.

Akkar & Co didn’t just out-execute Tripoli Boutique. It built a genuine edge, told the truth about it loudly, and then bought the one thing its own strength couldn’t manufacture: a customer base built entirely on old-fashioned, human trust.

Closing thought

Akkar & Co’s bet was the right one. Superior processes, encoded deliberately rather than smoothed away by a generic system, turned out to be worth defending — and when AI arrived, that decision didn’t just hold up, it paid out. Tripoli Boutique’s caution wasn’t foolish, exactly. It was simply insufficient: a safe choice that kept the lights on but never gave the company anything to amplify when the moment came.

And here’s the detail that makes the whole plan feel like design, not luck: both companies had been running the same ERP platform all along, just configured differently, so the integration itself was almost frictionless by construction. After the deal closed, Akkar & Co brought the vendor back to the table, not to ask whether the two systems could talk to each other, but to decide how deliberately Tripoli Boutique’s data should be folded in. They chose to merge it fully into Akkar & Co’s customized core, rather than bolt it on as a separate system, precisely so that Tripoli Boutique’s 20 years of purchase history could run directly through Akkar & Co’s optimized processes and AI models — not sit beside them as an afterthought but become part of the same intelligence from day one.

But sit with the ending for a second longer. What Akkar & Co actually acquired wasn’t a smaller retailer’s revenue — it was 20 years of trust that wealthy customers placed in people who knew them by name, and it’s about to run that trust through a machine built to predict what those same customers will want to buy next. The strategy worked exactly as designed. That’s not the uncomfortable part. The uncomfortable part is this: once a relationship built on being known becomes a dataset built on being predicted, is it still the same relationship — and does it matter, to the business or to the customer, if nobody involved can quite say when the answer changed?

item.title: AI spend will jump 49.5% in 2026, says Gartner
item.description:
Worldwide AI spending will increase 49.5% in 2026, to $2.7 trillion, and grow another 36.2% in 2027 as AI usage continues to expand, Gartner predicts in the latest quarterly update to its IT spending forecast.

But there’s been no diversion of money from other areas of IT to feed AI, said Gartner Distinguished VP Analyst John-David Lovelock. CIOs got some net new money for AI back in 2024, and a little in 2025, he said, “so there wasn’t a diversion, and now more of their spending is about rebranding than diversion.”

By 2030, “every dollar is going to be an AI dollar in one way or another,” he said.

Instead of buying just a laptop, companies now buy a laptop with AI chips in it, while enterprise software now has AI embedded in it. And instead of doing a project about business strategy, they now do a project about how AI might change business strategy.

“In one way, it’s kind of rebranding,” he said. “Net new spending is going more towards AI, and existing spending is being transformed towards AI.”

It’s similar with hyperscalers: “The hyperscalers haven’t diverted one dime away from their cloud. So AWS, Google, Microsoft, Meta are all continuing to build out their cloud infrastructure at the same rate they were in 2022.”

The AI buildout “is the largest infrastructure project humanity has ever undertaken,” he observed.

Gartner updates its spending forecasts quarterly. In its latest report, it predicted AI infrastructure spend will grow 51.2% this year, and AI software 60.2%. Spend on AI agents and assistants, which it breaks out separately from other software, is forecast to increase by 77.3%, and AI security spend to almost double.

As AI development platforms prove themselves, Gartner sees spending on them accelerating: It has increased its 2026 growth forecast for them from 28% in its May report to 39%, attributing the change to the development of custom AI applications by enterprises and software and service providers.

AI model providers are seeing a “small but growing opportunity” for domain-specific language models aligned with enterprise use cases, upping the 2026 growth rate for generative AI models to 117%.

Semiconductor surprise

But what surprised Lovelock was the semiconductor spend.

“Semiconductors for the last 30 years has been a nice, easy market to work through,” he said. “Total spending has been very incremental. It’s followed a nice long-term evolutionary curve. Back in 2015, we said it would be about a trillion dollars by 2030, and we got real pushback on that back then, saying we didn’t understand Moore’s law and fabrication and all the rest of it. Well, turns out both myself and the people giving the criticism were wrong, because with AI, chips are now going to push $2 trillion by 2030.”

The culprit is memory.

“We were ready for the run-up in the chips that went into the heart and soul of the servers. However, as the AI servers got more functional, they required more memory and, of course, more storage, which is also memory,” he said.

People often mistake the reason for the substantial rise in memory prices, he said: “It’s very often written that there is a memory shortage, which is not putting the blame or the explanation in the right place. There is a massive over-demand towards memory, and that’s pushed these chip prices incredibly high, and that has spiked that semiconductor spend, now doubling 2030 spend from what we thought it was before AI.”

His message to CIOs is straightforward: “The next two years, next three years, have at least three major transitions in them,” he said. “If you think you know what will happen with AI based on what is happening with AI, you’re wrong. The technology is changing too quickly for anybody to have assurances or certainty on what can be done and at what price point. This is going to be continually on your plate, and your balance between risk and reward has got to be your number one priority.”
